title: Demoralized But Not Defeated: What 2,000 Young Men Told IFS About Their Lives
gist: IFS's second installment of America's Demoralized Men, from a YouGov survey of 2,000 nationally representative men aged 18-29, finds roughly half of young men lonely or isolated, 4 in 10 with two or fewer close friends, half doubting the American Dream, and extraordinarily high daily rates of gambling (23%), gaming (44%) and pornography use (42% daily/several-times-weekly) — with each of those behaviors strongly correlated to feeling like a failure.

insights.claim: 43% of young men aged 18-29 agree they are inclined to think they are a failure, making self-assessed failure close to a plurality condition rather than a fringe outcome.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A baseline failure-sentiment rate of 42-43% is the control group against which every behavioral correlation in this report should be read.
insights.quote: I am inclined to think that I am a failure
insights.locator: “Demoralized” is the term we use

insights.claim: 61% of young men say they often feel they have little control over the things that happen to them — external locus of control is now the majority position among 18-29 year-old American men.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Perceived powerlessness at this scale is the psychological substrate for both lottery-style risk-taking and political volatility in a large voting and consumer bloc.
insights.quote: I often feel that I have little control over the things that happen to me
insights.locator: “Demoralized” is the term we use

insights.claim: 54% of young men agree that they never seem to do enough to please people, indicating that demoralization is driven by perceived insufficiency against others' expectations, not only by material outcomes.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Suggests status anxiety, not just income, drives the malaise — relevant to how status-goods and self-improvement spending among young men behaves.
insights.quote: I never seem to do enough to please people
insights.locator: “Demoralized” is the term we use

insights.claim: 48% of young men report lacking community much of the time, roughly double the shares reporting outright loneliness (25%) or isolation (26%) — community deficit is a bigger and distinct problem from loneliness.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Community deficit, not loneliness, is the larger addressable market; product and policy responses aimed only at 'loneliness' target half the problem.
insights.locator: We also report here on the dispiriting experience

insights.claim: The distribution of young men is bimodal rather than uniformly bleak: the authors explicitly note some young men are not in crisis but thriving while others struggle mightily.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Averages mislead here; the investable and policy-relevant story is a widening dispersion within a single cohort, not a uniform decline.
insights.quote: are not in crisis but thriving
insights.locator: As we noted in Part I

insights.claim: Four out of ten young men have two or fewer close friends, including 34% with one to two and 9% who report zero close friends.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A 9% zero-friend rate among 18-29 men quantifies the addressable base for male-oriented community, gaming and parasocial products.
insights.locator: For many young men friendships are in short supply

insights.claim: The single best predictor of a young man having three or more close friends is connection to institutions — marriage, church, and school — rather than personality, income, or online activity.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Institutional membership is the causal lever on male social capital; any thesis about rebuilding male community that skips institutions is mispriced.
insights.quote: The best predictor of having three or more friends is connection to institutions like marriage, church, and school.
insights.locator: For many young men friendships are in short supply

insights.claim: Participation in all-male groups such as sports teams or the Boy Scouts during school years is associated with markedly more friends in adulthood: 64% report three or more friends versus 48% of those who did not participate.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A 16-point durable spread from a childhood intervention — a concrete argument for youth-sports and scouting participation as long-lived social infrastructure.
insights.locator: Young men who participated in all-male groups

insights.claim: Formal civic participation among young men is thin across every category: 31% volunteer, 29% belong to a faith-based group, 27% to a social club, 24% to an adult sports league, though 57% do at least one community activity.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Quantifies the collapse of the membership-organization model that once monetized male affiliation; the 57%/31% gap shows most participation is shallow.
insights.locator: Social, civic, and religious participation is low

insights.claim: Community participation clusters tightly with a handful of statuses — being religious (81%), having finished trade school (74%), being a student (73%), or being married with kids (72%) — so participation is a byproduct of role, not disposition.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Trade-school completion tracking alongside religiosity and marriage as a social-integration marker is a non-obvious data point favoring vocational-education theses.
insights.locator: In terms of overall participation

insights.claim: Religiosity among young men is not uniformly decaying: 25% attend religious services at least monthly and 28% say they have become more religious in recent years.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A 28% self-reported religiosity uptick among young men is a counter-trend to secularization narratives and a leading indicator for faith-adjacent institutions.
insights.locator: Overall, 25% attend religious services

insights.claim: About half of young men agree that no matter how hard they work, people like them will never achieve the American Dream — the meritocratic story functions as a myth for a significant share of the cohort.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Half a male generation discounting the returns to effort is a structural input to political risk, populism, and risk-seeking financial behavior.
insights.quote: No matter how hard I work, people like me will never achieve the American Dream.
insights.locator: The American dream feels out of reach

insights.claim: 72% of young men agree that who you know is more important than ability or hard work in getting ahead, meaning belief in network capture over merit is now near-consensus.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A 72% belief in nepotism-over-merit predicts demand for credential shortcuts, alternative-status routes, and hostility to incumbent institutions.
insights.quote: Who you know is more important than ability or hard work in getting ahead
insights.locator: The American dream feels out of reach

insights.claim: Despite widespread pessimism about the system, 84% of young men say having ambitious plans for the future describes them at least somewhat well — they have lost faith in the pathway, not in themselves.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'checked-out young men' narrative: the deficit is pathway and structure, so interventions that supply legible routes should convert well.
insights.quote: a remarkable 84% say that having ambitious plans for the future describes them at least somewhat well
insights.locator: Highlights

insights.claim: 12% of young men aged 18-29 have ever been incarcerated, and 44% have had a loved one go to prison (28%), die of a drug overdose (18%), die by suicide (16%), or die by homicide (14%).
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Nearly half of a national male cohort carrying proximate trauma is an underpriced driver of healthcare utilization, disability claims and labor-force detachment.
insights.locator: A notable share of young men report having faced traumatic events

insights.claim: Trauma-exposed young men carry roughly double the psychiatric diagnosis rates of their peers: depression 49% vs 27%, anxiety disorder 44% vs 25%, ADHD 36% vs 19%, bipolar disorder 26% vs 8%, and learning disability 21% vs 11%.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: The bipolar gap (3x) and overall doubling quantify a concentrated, identifiable high-utilization segment for behavioral-health services and pharma demand.
insights.locator: The men with such experiences have higher rates

themes.theme: The Digital Vice Stack: Gambling, Gaming, Porn

insights.claim: Daily gambling among young men has reached 23%, with a further 12% gambling several times a week and 21% weekly or less — well over half the cohort gambles at some frequency.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A 23% daily-gambling rate in the core 18-29 male demographic is the single most consequential number here for sportsbook and prediction-market revenue durability — and for regulatory tail risk.
insights.quote: Gambling is rampant: 23% of young men gamble daily
insights.locator: Electronic media use is very high

insights.claim: Video gaming is near-universal and extremely heavy: 44% of young men play many times a day or more, and another 42% play at least a few times a week.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: 86% of young men gaming weekly-or-more with 44% at many-times-daily intensity underwrites engagement assumptions for gaming and in-game monetization.
insights.locator: Gaming is also very common

insights.claim: Pornography consumption is extremely widespread among young men: 42% watch daily (27%) or several times a week (16%), with another 26% viewing weekly or less.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Roughly two-thirds usage penetration is the backdrop for age-verification legislation and the platform-liability fights that follow.
insights.quote: Pornography use among young men is extremely widespread: 42% watch porn daily or several times a week, with another 26% viewing it weekly or less.
insights.locator: Highlights

insights.claim: Pornography use cuts across the institutional protections that predict other good outcomes: 21% of married young men and 24% of regular religious service attenders watch porn daily.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Marriage and churchgoing do not insulate against this behavior, so age-verification and content policy exposure is not confined to an unattached fringe.
insights.quote: Those who watch porn daily include married men (21%) and regular religious service attenders (24%).
insights.locator: Electronic media use is very high

insights.claim: Around two in three regular online gamblers say gambling has caused them at least some distress, meaning self-reported harm is the majority experience among the product's most active users.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Majority-harm self-reporting among heavy users is precisely the evidence base regulators and plaintiffs' lawyers use — a forward risk for gambling operator multiples.
insights.locator: Online gambling and pornography have significant emotional repercussions

insights.claim: Among young men who watch pornography many times a day or more, 43% experience loneliness, 36% feel depressed, and 29% are anxious.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Quantifies the psychological cost curve of heavy use that will anchor future litigation and regulation of adult platforms.
insights.locator: Of those who watch pornography many times a day

insights.claim: Feeling like a failure is concentrated in compulsive digital behaviors: 66% of daily gamblers and 63% of daily pornography watchers report feeling like a failure versus 42% of young men overall.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A ~21-24 point spread over baseline links the highest-margin digital vice products to measurable demoralization — the causal claim that drives policy action.
insights.quote: 66% of daily gamblers and 63% of daily pornography watchers, compared to 42% of men as a whole, report feeling like a failure
insights.locator: Online gambling and pornography have significant emotional repercussions

insights.claim: Young men define adulthood in terms of personal responsibility, self-direction, and financial independence, yet judge their own adult status by older markers — marriage, parenthood, and finishing school — so many conclude they have not reached full adulthood.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: The dual-standard explains why traditional life-stage consumption (housing, autos, durables) lags income among young men: they don't self-identify as adults yet.
insights.locator: In Part I, we began our exploration

insights.claim: The great majority of young men express a strong desire to be responsible, earn enough to support others, date, marry, and become fathers — the deficit is in attainment, not aspiration.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Latent demand for family formation is intact, so the marriage and fertility downturn is a friction story that policy or economics could partly unwind.
insights.locator: However, when we asked about work, manhood, marriage

insights.claim: Young men name specific blockers to their goals — inadequate incomes, limits on educational opportunity, personal struggles, and difficulty finding a suitable romantic partner — and the gap between aspiration and position is itself the source of frustration and stress.
insights.speaker: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Identifies four distinct friction points; income and partner-search are the two most tractable to market solutions.
insights.locator: Reaching these worthy goals, however, is another matter
